profile.headline: Software Engineer at Dropbox
profile.summary:
I am currently a software engineer at Dropbox on the infrastructure team, currently focusing on developing infra for provisioning, using, and managing VMs and containers at scale. I have a combine Bachelor's and Master's degree in computer science from the University of Washington.

I have a pretty wide spread of interests in science, technology, and computer science: I've tinkered with a variety of different things ranging from hardware and electronics to web development. But currently, I'm specifically interested in programming languages/static analysis and on CS pedagogy. 

For example, I periodically contribute to mypy, an open source static type checker for Python and coauthored PEP 586. You can see some of my pull requests here:

- https://github.com/python/mypy/pulls?q=is%3Apr+author%3AMichael0x2a+is%3Aclosed

I also like spending time answering questions and sharing knowledge both on StackOverflow and reddit. You can check out my answers (and my writing) here:

- http://stackoverflow.com/users/646543/michael0x2a
- https://www.reddit.com/user/michael0x2a?sort=top

I'm currently not looking for a new job, but if you have a particularly compelling one that you think is aligned with my interests or would be a great learning opportunity, feel free to reach out.

positions.title: Software Engineer
positions.description:
I work on infrastructure at Dropbox, focusing specifically on infra for provisioning, using, and managing VMs and containers at scale. More generally, the subteam I'm a part of specializes in creating systems that cleanly abstract and manage the boundaries between software engineers and lower-level details like operating systems, host management, virtualization technologies, and so forth.

My previous project focused on transforming the process for provisioning VMs from a partly-automated process that required frequent manual interventions to an actually automated, deterministic, robust, and low KTLO process.

My current project is focusing on rethinking and streamlining how we use these VMs for both continuous integration and local development.

positions.title: Instructor
positions.description:
During Winter quarter, I taught CSE 373, the non-major's data structures and algorithms course. Our course consisted of approximately 200 students who attended hour-long lectures three times a week. I also oversaw a team of 8 TAs who taught additional hour-long supplemental "sections" of 20-30 students once a week.

I also took a sabbatical during Summer 2017 to redesign and overhaul the assignments, section handouts, and course infrastructure from scratch. 

Specifically, the assignments were modified to:

- Be more challenging: students were asked to apply data structures they implemented to complete relatively non-trivial projects (a symbolic calculator, a search engine, and a maze solver/generator) and to complete analytical write-ups.
- Give students practice both implementing and using data structures in an applied context. Past quarters only asked students to do the former.
- Expose students to industry best-practices: using industry-strength IDEs such as Eclipse or IntelliJ, using and writing JUnit tests, using style linters, pair-programming, etc...

The TA-led section handouts were also overhauled to include a wider variety of problems to give TAs more flexibility on what material they wanted to cover during the section and to give students more practice problems.

These changes were trial-run by another instructor in Autumn 2017 before I taught in Winter 2018; they were subsequently adopted by the next instructor in Spring 2018.

You can see my course materials (and recordings of my lectures) here: https://courses.cs.washington.edu/courses/cse373/18wi/

positions.title: Computer Science Teaching Assistant
positions.description:
I was a teaching assistant (TA) for multiple computer science classes at the University of Washington. The specific classes I taught include:

‒ CSE 142: Our CS 1 equivalent, focusing on programming fundamentals and Java
‒ CSE 143: Our CS 2 equivalent, focusing on OOP and basic data structures
‒ CSE 311: Introduction to discrete math and proofs
‒ CSE 332: Data structures, algorithms, and a dash of parallelism

General TA responsibilities include teaching hour-long weekly sessions to about 20-25 students, holding office hours, and helping grade assignments and exams.

Some things that I've specifically done at one point or another are:

‒ Answered the vast majority of students' questions on our message board. Students in the larger classes ask ~1000-1200 questions per quarter; I maintained an average response time of about 10-11 minutes.
‒ Oversaw and coordinated grading for all TAs for a course
‒ Helped develop and prototype new assignments
‒ Authored a 100+ page-long style guide for CSE 142 and 143, containing in-depth justifications and examples of each rule to try and help students "grok" why clean code matters.
‒ Developed an automated style grader that can detect assignment-specific anti-patterns by pattern-matching on specific AST shapes and type patterns. 
‒ Won the Bob Bandes Award for Excellence in Teaching (2015-2016).

I was also a head TA in either a formal or informal capacity for most of these courses. My duties mainly involved wrangling other TAs, coordinating grading consistency, and putting out weekly fires.

positions.title: Electronics Team
positions.description:
I was a member of the Electronics technical team and Resources admin team on the UW Formula Motorsports team. 

UW formula is a student-run organization comprising of around 80-90 members that designs, manufactures, and races formula-style combustion and electric racecars. Our team is internationally ranked 7th out of 500+ teams.

I was mainly responsible for designing and implementing the telemetry software. The software was implemented in Python with a custom JavaScript frontend, and communicated with the cars in real-time using paired ZigBee radios. I also redesigned their website on top of the Bolt CMS.

positions.title: Software Engineering Intern
positions.description:
This summer, I was an intern at Dropbox where I worked on Mypy, an open-source static analysis tool that can perform gradual type checking against Python code. Mypy is currently in beta and is going through active development and refinement. You can find more info on the project website:

http://www.mypy-lang.org/

My main project this summer was to work on improving the performance and speed of Mypy, specifically focusing on incremental mode. When run in incremental mode, Mypy will attempt to reuse the results of previous runs when performing typechecking to avoid repeating extra work.

Incremental mode was already implemented when I arrived at Dropbox, but was inconsistent and buggy in a variety of ways, typically relating to imports and convoluted import cycles. Over the summer, I...

‒ Focused on fixing a variety of incremental/import related bugs and inefficiencies
‒ Rewrote a part of the caching layer to allow the checker to recheck a smaller number of imports
‒ Contributed related tests and tools for checking incremental mode

Beyond working on incremental mode, I contributed misc documentation enhancements, bug fixes, and minor features.

positions.title: Web developer
positions.description:
I was one of the volunteers helping to organize TEDxUofW at the University of Washington where I focused primarily on...

‒ Modernizing and renovating our website
‒ Integrating the website cohesively with our marketing and social media campaign
‒ Transforming our website into a comprehensive portfolio and retrospective of past events

The website (http://tedxuofw.com) changes each year to match the theme of that year's conference. The source code for all past years can be found on github at https://github.com/tedxuofw. I built the website using a combination of Twitter Bootstrap, Jekyll, and SASS.

TED is an an organization dedicated to spreading ideas from a large variety of fields, usually in the form of short, 18-20 minute talks. TEDx is a locally-organized version of TED.

positions.title: Software Engineering Intern
positions.description:
Over the summer, I interned with the Developer Relations team for Google Cloud Platform.

My summer project was to work an on open-source transpiler to convert arbitrary Apache Pig scripts into Java programs using the Google Dataflow SDK. 

(For context, Pig is a scripting language/DSL used to perform ad-hoc data analysis on datasets -- the language is sort of similar to SQL, except imperative instead of declarative. Pig scripts can be run both locally and as Hadoop jobs. Dataflow is a product Google recently produced which is intended to be the successor of MapReduce, and is intended to greatly simplify the process of working with absurdly large datasets.)

The ultimate goal of this project was to provide an easy migration path for people who have a large amount of Pig scripts onto Google Cloud Platform.

Besides working on my main project, I also helped identify and fill in missing information and other gaps in both our documentation and general toolchain/open-source ecosystem for Dataflow.

positions.title: Software Engineering Intern
positions.description:
During the summer, I was a member of the Goods Logistics team at their Seattle office.

I mainly worked together with another intern to build a dashboard for internal and merchant use that collects information and presents a real-time aggregate summary on every purchase order and sales order within Groupon Goods.

The dashboard was designed primarily to be used by business users and merchants to help get a better feel for the orders flowing through Goods and to help easily diagnose any issues with specific orders. 

The backend, which is responsible for accessing and splicing together data from the other internal Groupon services, is written in Java Play 2.x, using Memcache to help alleviate the load. It presents a REST-ful API which is then consumed by our frontend to display the data in a friendly format. The frontend uses a blend of Angular.js, Bootstrap, and d3 (for visualizations).

positions.title: Research Intern
positions.description:
I interned at Microsoft Research (MSR) during the summer of my Junior and Senior year in high school. Specifically, I worked at the "Conversational Systems Research Center", which is a team within MSR studying Spoken Language Understanding (SLU) under Xiaodong He and Li Deng.

During the summer of my Junior year, I...

‒ Developed a parser using Python and Pyparsing to convert a formalized subset of English commands into SQL queries. The final product had a success rate of ~70%.
‒ Programmed smaller tools and utilities to help analyze data, generate statistics, and assist other interns, helping improve overall productivity by ~20%.
‒ Manually annotated and labelled 13k search queries for machine learning, providing a dataset that helped lead to a ~10% improvement in experimental search algorithms

I was invited back into the Conversational Systems Research Center at Microsoft Research for my senior year. My partner and I...

‒ Developed a tool using C# that analyzed and answered arbitrary English questions regarding flight and travel (end-to-end evaluation) with a success rate of ~98%, 
‒ Wrote a 50-60 page report documenting our project and various inconsistencies and flaws we found in the dataset we used.

Our program and report is anticipated to be used as part of research paper on the effectiveness of the 'tagging' approach to natural language parsing as opposed to the 'semantic tree' approach. .

You can try it out at http://wingman.azurewebsites.net

positions.title: Club President, Programming/Electronics team Captain, Website Design/Maintenance team Captain
positions.description:
I joined my high school's FIRST robotics team (team 2976) in Sophomore year, and became the de-facto programming/electronics team captain. I was subsequently elected as the club president during my Junior and Senior year, and continued to serve as the programming/electronics lead as well as the website lead.

As club president, I:

‒ Rebuilt and rebooted the club from scratch in Junior year after all club members with any experience graduated
‒ Focused on setting up systems and practices to ensure information and experience would be preserved after core members graduate
‒ Led a team to build competitive robots under short 6 week deadlines
‒ Managed and directed 20-30 students, planned logistics and transportation, recruited mentors, and planned long-term and short-term logistics
‒ Helped raise, budget, and manage $15,000+ from grants and fundraisers annually

As the programming/electronics lead, I developed the bulk of the codebase, mentored incoming students, and wired and debugged all electrical components on the robot.

I joined my high school's FIRST robotics team (team 2976) in Sophomore year, and became the de-facto programming/electronics team captain. I was subsequently elected as the club president during my Junior and Senior year, and continued to serve as the programming/electronics lead as well as the website lead.

As club president, I:

‒ Rebuilt and rebooted the club from scratch in Junior year after all club members with any experience graduated
‒ Focused on setting up systems and practices to ensure information and experience would be preserved after core members graduate
‒ Led a team to build competitive robots under short 6 week deadlines
‒ Managed and directed 20-30 students, planned logistics and transportation, recruited mentors, and planned long-term and short-term logistics
‒ Helped raise, budget, and manage $15,000+ from grants and fundraisers annually

As the programming/electronics lead, I developed the bulk of the codebase, mentored incoming students, and wired and debugged all electrical components on the robot.
experience.position: Club President, Programming/Electronics team Captain, Website Design/Maintenance team Captain
